questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the ratio that uses the side adjacent to angle θ and the hypotenuse is:
questions.explanation: cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Writing hypotenuse/adjacent inverts the cosine ratio.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, the side labelled a is:
options: the side next to angle A
the side between angles A and B
questions.explanation: By convention the lower-case letter names the side opposite the angle with the same capital letter. The side between angles A and B is c, opposite angle C.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 12 cm and an angle of 35°. The side opposite the 35° angle, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: sin 35° = opposite/12, so opposite = 12 sin 35° = 6.88 cm. Using cos gives 9.83 cm, which is the adjacent side.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has the side opposite θ equal to 5 m and the side adjacent to θ equal to 8 m. The angle θ, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: tan θ = 5/8, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.625) = 32.0°. Using sin⁻¹(5/8) gives 38.7°, which treats 8 m as the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has a 40° angle with an adjacent side of 15 cm. The hypotenuse, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: cos 40° = 15/h, so h = 15 ÷ cos 40° = 19.58 cm. Multiplying instead, 15 cos 40° = 11.49, gives a length shorter than a side, which a hypotenuse cannot be.

questions.stem: A wheelchair ramp rises 1.2 m over a horizontal distance of 9 m. The angle the ramp makes with the horizontal, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The rise and horizontal run are opposite and adjacent, so θ = tan⁻¹(1.2/9) = 7.6°. Using sin⁻¹ gives 7.7°, which wrongly treats 9 m as the length of the sloping ramp.

questions.stem: A surveyor measures an angle of elevation to the top of a mast. This angle is measured:
options: clockwise from true north to the line of sight
upwards from the horizontal to the line of sight
downwards from the horizontal to the line of sight
upwards from the vertical to the line of sight
questions.explanation: Elevation is the angle up from the horizontal to an object above the observer; depression is the angle down from the horizontal. Clockwise from north describes a true bearing.

questions.stem: The angle of elevation from point P to point Q is 25°. The angle of depression from Q to P is:
questions.explanation: Both angles are measured from horizontal lines, which are parallel, so they are alternate angles and equal. The value 65° measures from the vertical instead.

questions.stem: From a point 50 m from the base of a tower on level ground, the angle of elevation of its top is 32°. The height of the tower, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: tan 32° = h/50, so h = 50 tan 32° = 31.2 m. Using sin gives 26.5 m, which treats 50 m as the line of sight rather than the ground distance.

questions.stem: From the top of an 80 m cliff, the angle of depression to a boat is 18°. The horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff to the boat, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The angle at the boat equals the angle of depression, 18°, so tan 18° = 80/d and d = 80 ÷ tan 18° = 246.2 m. The value 258.9 m is the line-of-sight distance 80 ÷ sin 18°.

questions.stem: A pole 4 m tall casts a shadow 5.5 m long on level ground. The angle of elevation of the sun, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: tan θ = 4/5.5, so θ = 36.0°. The value 54.0° is the angle at the top of the pole, measured from the vertical.

questions.stem: From a point on level ground, the angle of elevation of the top of a building is 30°. After walking 40 m directly towards it, the angle is 45°. The height of the building, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: With height h, the distances are h/tan 30° = h√3 and h/tan 45° = h, so h√3 − h = 40 and h = 40/(√3 − 1) = 54.6 m. The value 94.6 m is the first distance from the building, not the height.

questions.stem: From the top of a 60 m lighthouse, the angles of depression to two boats due east of it are 30° and 20°. The distance between the boats, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The boats are 60 ÷ tan 30° = 103.9 m and 60 ÷ tan 20° = 164.8 m from the base, so they are 164.8 − 103.9 = 60.9 m apart. The other two values are the separate distances from the lighthouse.

questions.stem: True bearings are measured:
options: anticlockwise from north, written with three digits
clockwise from east, written with three digits
from north or south towards east or west
clockwise from north, written with three digits
questions.explanation: A true bearing such as 070°T is the angle turned clockwise from true north. Measuring from north or south towards east or west describes compass bearings like N70°E, a different system.

questions.stem: The true bearing of the direction south-west is:
questions.explanation: South is 180°T and south-west is a further 45° clockwise, giving 225°T. South-east is 135°T and north-west is 315°T.

questions.stem: The bearing of B from A is 070°T. The bearing of A from B is:
questions.explanation: The reverse bearing differs by 180°: 070° + 180° = 250°T. Subtracting from 180° gives 110°T, which is not the opposite direction.

questions.stem: A hiker walks 6 km on a bearing of 090°T and then 8 km on a bearing of 180°T. The bearing of the hiker's finish from the start, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The finish is 6 km east and 8 km south, so its angle east of south is tan⁻¹(6/8) = 36.9°, and the bearing is 180° − 36.9° = 143.1°T. The value 323.1°T is the bearing of the start from the finish.

questions.stem: A ship sails 12 km on a bearing of 050°T. How far north of its starting point is it, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The bearing is the angle from north, so the northward component is 12 cos 50° = 7.71 km. The eastward component is 12 sin 50° = 9.19 km.

questions.stem: A hiker walks 5 km on a bearing of 060°T, then turns and walks 8 km on a bearing of 150°T. The bearing of the hiker's finish from the start, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The turn from 060° to 150° is 90°, so the legs form a right angle; the angle at the start between the first leg and the finish is tan⁻¹(8/5) = 58.0°, so the bearing is 060° + 58.0° = 118.0°T. The value 298.0°T is the reverse bearing.

questions.stem: Using area = (1/2)bc sin A, the area of a triangle with b = 8 cm, c = 11 cm and A = 30° is:
questions.explanation: Area = (1/2) × 8 × 11 × sin 30° = 44 × 0.5 = 22 cm². Using cos 30° instead of sin 30° gives 38.1 cm².

questions.stem: Which method finds the area of a triangle when only its three side lengths are known?
questions.explanation: Heron's rule uses only the three sides, through s = (a + b + c)/2. The formula (1/2)bc sin A needs an included angle, and (1/2)bh needs a perpendicular height.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 7 m and 10 m with an included angle of 120°. Its area, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: Area = (1/2) × 7 × 10 × sin 120° = 35 × 0.866 = 30.3 m². Forgetting the half gives 60.6 m², and using the size of cos 120° gives 17.5 m².

questions.stem: Using Heron's rule, the area of a triangle with sides 5 m, 6 m and 7 m, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: s = (5 + 6 + 7)/2 = 9, so area = √(9 × 4 × 3 × 2) = √216 = 14.7 m². The value 216.0 forgets the square root, and 175.7 uses the full perimeter 18 instead of s.

questions.stem: A triangular paddock has sides 13 m, 14 m and 15 m. Its area is:
questions.explanation: s = 21, so by Heron's rule the area is √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84 m². The value 7056 leaves out the square root.

questions.stem: A triangle has area 30 cm² and sides of 8 cm and 10 cm enclosing an acute angle. That angle, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: 30 = (1/2) × 8 × 10 × sin θ gives sin θ = 0.75, so θ = 48.6°. The obtuse angle 131.4° has the same sine but is excluded because the angle is acute.

questions.stem: A triangle has area 24 cm², a side b = 8 cm and angle A = 30°. Using area = (1/2)bc sin A, the side c is:
questions.explanation: 24 = (1/2) × 8 × c × 0.5 = 2c, so c = 12 cm. Forgetting the half gives 24 = 4c and c = 6 cm.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, the sine rule states that:
options: a sin A = b sin B = c sin C
a/sin B = b/sin C = c/sin A
sin A + sin B + sin C = a + b + c
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
questions.explanation: Each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same value. Pairing a side with a different angle, such as a with sin B, breaks the rule.

questions.stem: Which information calls for the cosine rule, rather than the sine rule, to find the third side of a triangle?
options: Two angles and any one side
Two sides and an angle opposite one of them
Two sides and the angle between them
questions.explanation: With two sides and the included angle, no side is paired with its opposite angle, so the sine rule cannot start; the cosine rule is needed. Two angles and a side suit the sine rule, and three angles fix only the shape.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 65° and a = 12 cm. The length of b, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: b/sin 65° = 12/sin 40°, so b = 12 sin 65° ÷ sin 40° = 16.92 cm. Swapping the sines gives 8.51 cm, but b must be longer than a because B is larger than A.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, a = 9 cm, b = 7 cm and A = 50°. Angle B, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: sin B = 7 sin 50° ÷ 9 = 0.596, so B = 36.6°. B must be smaller than A because b < a, which rules out the obtuse 143.4°; 80.0° comes from inverting the ratio.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, A = 35°, B = 75° and c = 20 m. The length of a, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: First C = 180° − 35° − 75° = 70°, then a = 20 sin 35° ÷ sin 70° = 12.21 m. Dividing by sin 75° gives 11.88, which pairs c with the wrong angle.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, the side c is found from sides a and b and angle C by:
questions.explanation: The angle used is the one opposite the side being found, and the term 2ab cos C is subtracted. With C = 90° the rule becomes Pythagoras' theorem.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, a = 7 cm, b = 9 cm and C = 60°. The length of c, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: c² = 49 + 81 − 2 × 7 × 9 × cos 60° = 130 − 63 = 67, so c = 8.19 cm. Leaving out the 2ab cos C term gives √130 = 11.40, as if the angle were 90°.

questions.stem: A triangular sail has edges of 5 m, 7 m and 8 m. The angle opposite the 7 m edge is:
questions.explanation: cos θ = (5² + 8² − 7²)/(2 × 5 × 8) = 40/80 = 0.5, so θ = 60°. The angles 38.2° and 81.8° are opposite the 5 m and 8 m edges.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 4 m, 6 m and 9 m. Its largest angle, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The largest angle is opposite the 9 m side: cos θ = (16 + 36 − 81)/48 = −29/48, so θ = 127.2°. Dropping the negative sign gives 52.8°, an acute angle that cannot be opposite the longest side here.

questions.stem: Two ships leave port together. One sails 20 km on a bearing of 040°T and the other 30 km on a bearing of 150°T. The distance between them, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The angle between the courses is 150° − 40° = 110°, so d² = 400 + 900 − 1200 cos 110° = 1710.4 and d = 41.4 km. Using Pythagoras gives 36.1 km, which would need a 90° angle.

questions.stem: Two sides of a triangular garden are 12 m and 15 m, with an included angle of 52°. The perimeter of the garden, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The third side is √(144 + 225 − 360 cos 52°) = 12.14 m, so the perimeter is 12 + 15 + 12.14 = 39.1 m. The value 46.2 m uses Pythagoras for the third side, and 12.1 m is the third side alone.
